extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, creative-writing students, and literary critics interested in narrative theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting and evaluating fictional narrative as a form of rhetoric — how choices of voice, POV, ordering, and narration persuade readers and shape ethical effects. Useful for writers shaping narrative strategy and critics assessing narrative stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative as rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: All narrative is rhetoric. Authors persuade audiences through structural choices about what information to reveal and how to reveal it. There is no "neutral" telling — every choice (POV, ordering, voice) is rhetorically loaded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing or evaluating fiction, treat choices of POV, order, and voice as deliberate persuasive moves. Ask what position the text is trying to produce in the reader and whether each formal decision serves that rhetorical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implied author
rubrics_metrics.description: The "second self" of the author that readers construct from textual evidence — distinct from the flesh-and-blood writer. The implied author is "the sum of his own choices" within the work. A novel can have a generous implied author even if the real author is mean-spirited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the coherence and persona produced by the sum of the work's choices. Evaluate the implied author's values and how consistently they are signaled; distinguish those signs from biographical assumptions about the real author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrator reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator is unreliable when their account diverges from the implied author's norms. Reliability is judged against the values the work as a whole endorses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge reliability relative to the implied author's standards rather than absolute truth alone. Use detected divergence to interpret irony, satire, ethical distance, or psychological complexity; be alert to deliberate rhetorical uses of unreliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Showing vs. telling — rhetorical choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Booth rejected the modernist orthodoxy that "showing" is always superior to "telling." Both are necessary. Authors must select based on rhetorical purpose. Telling is sometimes the more honest, more efficient, and more powerful choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide between showing and telling according to effect, economy, and honesty of the narrative voice; avoid treating 'showing' as an automatic virtue or rule to follow without purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation of distance
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors manipulate distance between reader and characters along multiple axes: moral (alignment of values), intellectual (reader knowledge vs. character knowledge), physical/temporal (nearness in scene), and emotional (sympathy or detachment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how shifts in each axis of distance shape reader engagement and judgement. Use distance intentionally to control sympathy, suspense, dramatic irony, or critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of literary interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Three types of literary interest that a work may aim to satisfy: Intellectual — curiosity about facts, mysteries, truth; Qualitative — desire for pattern completion and aesthetic satisfaction; Practical — emotional investment in character outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify which type(s) of interest the work foregrounds and judge effectiveness by how well the narrative sustains and resolves that interest for readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of narration / narrator modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Varied axes of narration: dramatized vs. undramatized narrators; self-conscious vs. unself-conscious; privileged (omniscient) vs. limited; reliable vs. unreliable; observer vs. agent narrators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze the narrator across these dimensions to understand how information is framed and what stance the text invites. Select the narrator mode that best serves the work's rhetorical and ethical aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical criticism / moral effect
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel can be judged in part by the company it keeps the reader in — what kind of person it asks the reader to become while reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the ethical formation or solicited attitudes of readers as an evaluative criterion: consider the moral positions the work cultivates and whether those positions are endorsed, problematized, or ambiguously presented by the implied author.
